explanations.explanation:
1. References to respiratory support parameters and clinical metrics (e.g. FiO₂, ABG analysis, NIV).  
2. Naming of educational institutions in sports contexts (e.g. “Sacred Heart Prep,” “Menlo School”).  
3. Algebraic financial formulas computing cost, selling price and related quantities (e.g. CP, SP, DS, AS).  
4. Document posting metadata, notably “posted: [date] PDF document – [size]K.”  
5. Outline-style enumerations labeled with uppercase letters followed by a parenthesis (A), B), etc.).  
6. Regulatory or policy section headings formatted as “XX.XX – Title.”  
7. Discussion of GPS data and its inherent inaccuracies.  
8. Sports schedules listing home/away (A/H), date, time and opposing team.  
9. Baseball game reports including player jersey numbers in parentheses (e.g. “(#4)”).  
10. Corporate press‐release headers with location, date, company name and an “is pleased to announce” lead-in.  
11. Enumerated event coverage entries marked with numbers in parentheses (1), 2), 3), …).  
12. Product color option lists with color names qualified in parentheses.  
13. Press release headers showing stock‐exchange tickers, market‐wire sources and corporate identifiers.  
14. Team event schedules annotated with H/A codes, dates, times and venues for practices or tryouts.  
15. Soap-opera recap text pairing character names with actor names in parentheses.  
16. Academic presentation citations with date, co-authors in parentheses, title and venue details.  
17. Professional qualification notices specifying exam components labeled “Part I” and “Part II.”  
18. Academic data-table entries enumerating cells or footnote indices for sectors and statistics.  
19. Scientific text containing parenthetical literature citations of the form “Author et al. (Year).”

This feature fires on the punctuation that marks out numbered or sectioned list items—essentially the closing parenthesis (and adjacent formatting) used in enumeration tokens like “1)”, “2)”, “3)”, etc., signaling list‐item or section headers.

This neuron is not picking out ordinary prose but rather the little bits of “plumbing” around content—section‐headings, boilerplate metadata and source attributions.  It lights up on things like affiliate‐program names (“Associates Program”), RSS/feed links, “posted in…” blog tags, DOI numbers and journal names, correction notices (“inaccurately reported”), “Welcome” banners, publisher credits (“Published by…”) and so on.  In short, it flags structural/navigation labels and citation or attribution tokens rather than the main narrative text.

This neuron fires on the “root” of a top‐level clause or phrase—i.e. the main predicate (auxiliary, modal or full verb) or the head noun of an initial temporal/topic adverbial that anchors each sentence.

This neuron lights up on those little “easy‐does‐it” calls to action—simple, second-person imperatives like “simply…,” “find out…,” “click…,” etc., that reassure the reader and direct them to take a straightforward next step.
This neuron fires at the exact point where the model shifts from a “What…?” question into the start of its answer—i.e. it marks the opening token of the response segment.
This neuron flags the subordinating “When” at the start of a clause—i.e. the temporal/conditional “When X, …” construction that sets up a context or trigger for the following main statement.

This neuron is a simple “capitalized-subtoken” detector—it lights up on subword pieces that begin with an uppercase letter (especially the common name‐prefixes like Van, Mc, Sp etc., as well as drug or product names), effectively flagging the start of a proper noun or branded/model term.
This feature detects Markdown bold/emphasis spans—i.e. the double‐asterisk markers (`**…**`) and the words or punctuation they enclose, as used for headings or highlighted terms.

1. Boilerplate software‐license and copyright header text (dates, authors, warranty disclaimers).  
2. Descriptions of U.S. historical landmarks and their founding/signing significance.  
3. Taxonomic synonymy notices in biological classification (species synonyms, type designations).  
4. Academic research‐centre profiles with acronyms and enumerated disciplines.  
5. University course‐page/syllabus outlines with reading lists and organizational metadata.  
6. State eligibility/examination notices and application‐form eligibility criteria with expanded acronyms.  
7. Municipal environmental‐services division process descriptions (plan review, permitting, inspection).  
8. Nonprofit or center announcements (founders, awards, relocations, collaborative events).  
9. Hotel property descriptions: location, nearby attractions, and in-room amenities.  
10. Television program and schedule entries (show title, cast/crew credits, broadcast dates, taglines).  
11. Political‐corruption news reports on indicted legislators and related electoral details.  
12. Clinical‐genetics laboratory marketing copy listing test portfolios and diagnostic specialties.  
13. Biotech/drug‐development platform summaries outlining therapeutic modalities and pipelines.  
14. Legal‐case reportage concerning Native American remains under NAGPRA litigation.  
15. Local municipal bulletins on event openings and public‐space disruptions in a city.  
16. Workshop/conference registration pages: schedules, deadlines, forms, and program participation rules.  
17. Regional agricultural partnership announcements listing member organizations and service offerings.  
18. Music gig/event promotions: lineups, venues, ticket-purchase calls to action.  
19. Photography/exhibition closing notices with sponsor acknowledgments and grant credits.  
20. Biotech corporate press releases on FDA interactions, clinical-trial milestones, and conference attendance.
